interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you showed leadership without having any formal authority over the people involved.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A platform team I was part of wanted every service to adopt a new internal logging library, and one service team's lead was openly skeptical — his team had already built their own wrapper and saw no reason to switch. I had no authority over his team's roadmap.

In a short conversation I found his real objection wasn't the library's quality, it was migration cost eating into his sprint. Rather than argue the point, I offered to migrate one small, low-risk service myself as a pilot, timed it, and it took about two hours, not the sprint he feared. I didn't present the result to his team directly — I gave it to him and let him bring it to his own engineers as his own finding.

His team migrated within two weeks, and he went on to advocate for the library with two other skeptical teams I'd never spoken to — which is the part I'd call the actual leadership signal, since it kept spreading after I stopped being involved.

The mechanism I'd point to specifically: I removed the real objection with evidence instead of a counter-argument, and I let the message travel through someone his team already trusted rather than announcing it myself. Both mattered more than anything I said directly to him.

**Testing:** whether you can name a concrete influence mechanism — not just assert that persuasion happened — and whether the outcome required your continued presence to survive.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Influence

interviewQuestions.question: Describe a situation where you had to set direction on a problem no one had actually assigned to you.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Our team's on-call alerting had accumulated over two years with thresholds copy-pasted between services, and no single person accountable for whether any given alert was still useful. It wasn't in anyone's goals to fix — it just quietly cost every on-call engineer sleep.

No one asked me to take this on. I spent about a week auditing every active alert, tagging each one as still-useful, noisy, or dead, and found roughly 40% fell into the last two categories. I wrote up a proposed standard — every alert needs a named owner and a documented reason to page — and brought it to the three team leads whose services were most affected, along with the audit data so the scale of the problem wasn't just my opinion.

All three adopted the standard in the next planning cycle. The part I'd emphasize is the first move: nobody assigned this, and it would have been easy to notice the pattern and just complain about it in a retro instead of spending a week actually auditing it before asking anyone for anything.

What I took from it is that the hardest part of leading through ambiguity usually isn't the execution — it's deciding, unprompted, that a problem is worth your own unassigned time before you have any evidence anyone else will care.

**Testing:** whether you can identify and act on a genuinely unowned problem, versus only executing on ambiguous tasks you were explicitly handed.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Ambiguity

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you tried to influence someone and it didn't work.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I proposed consolidating two internal tools that did largely overlapping things, expecting the owning team to welcome offloading maintenance. They declined, citing concerns about losing ownership of a tool their team had built its identity around.

In hindsight, my mistake was sequencing: I'd already written the full proposal, including a migration plan, before looping them in — so by the time they saw it, it read as a decision made about their tool rather than a collaboration on a shared problem. I didn't force it after they said no; pushing a consolidation over an unwilling owning team tends to produce compliance without buy-in, which usually resurfaces as passive resistance later.

Six months after, I had a similar consolidation opportunity with a different pair of tools, and I changed the approach: I brought the *problem* — not a drafted solution — to both owning teams first, and built the actual proposal together with them. That one was adopted within a month.

What I'd want an interviewer to take from this: I can point to a real miss, name the specific process mistake that caused it rather than blaming the other team's stubbornness, and show that I changed my approach concretely afterward rather than repeating it or abandoning the tactic of influence altogether.

**Testing:** whether you have an honest failure prepared for this category, and whether your diagnosis of why it failed is genuinely self-critical rather than externalized.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Failed influence

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide when a problem is worth taking on informally versus escalating and asking for it to be formally assigned to someone?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I weigh two things: how much the problem's cost is already visible to the people who'd need to approve formal ownership, and how cheap it is for me to make meaningful progress before asking anyone for anything.

If the cost is already obvious — say, a recurring incident everyone's felt — I'll usually escalate early, because a formal owner with dedicated time will do better than my side-of-desk effort, and asking first avoids duplicated work if someone's already planning to tackle it. But if the cost is invisible until someone actually measures it — like the stale alerting problem, which nobody had quantified — I'll do the unglamorous, cheap-to-me legwork first: the audit, the rough cost estimate, a small pilot. That turns an abstract ask ("can someone own alerting hygiene") into a concrete one ("here's the 40% of alerts that are dead weight, and here's a standard three teams have already agreed would fix it").

The risk I actively watch for is spending real effort on something that turns out to be someone else's already-planned work, or that leadership would have deprioritized had I asked first — so I keep the initial investment small (days, not sprints) until I have some signal the direction is right.

**Testing:** whether you have real judgment about when informal initiative is the right tool versus when it's premature or duplicative — a distinctly staff-level calibration question.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Judgment
